intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to scale, impute and encode a feature, and spot both target leakage and preprocessing leakage.
intro.whyItMatters: Most models that score suspiciously well in a notebook have a leak.

recap.keyIdea: Features are scaled, filled and encoded with numbers learned from the training rows alone, and any column that is only known after the outcome has to be removed.

blocks.text: You rescaled a column by min-max and by standardising, filled a gap with the median of a skewed column, and turned a category into one-hot columns. Each step learned something from a set of rows, so each has to be fitted to the training rows only, and a column recorded after the outcome has to be dropped even though it scores brilliantly.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson builds the decision tree, a model that needs no scaling and chooses its splits by a number computed from counts.

lessons.title: Decision trees and ensembles

steps.headline: A tree node holds the training examples that reach it, and its Gini impurity measures how mixed they are.

lead.text: A decision tree makes a prediction by asking a series of yes-or-no questions about the features. Each question splits the examples into two groups, each group is split again, and a group that is no longer split is a leaf, which predicts the majority class among the examples in it. A node of ten loans in which seven were repaid and three were not is mixed, and a tree has to ask a question that makes the groups below it less mixed.

afterFigure.text: The measure used by the CART method, published by Leo Breiman, Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone in 1984, is the **Gini impurity**, **G = 1 − Σ p²**, where p is the share of each class in the node. A pure node has G = 0. For the node of seven and three, G = 1 − 0.7² − 0.3² = 1 − 0.49 − 0.09 = 0.42, and a node of five and five has the largest possible value for two classes, 0.5.

diagram.alt: Two views of Gini impurity. The first shows three nodes of ten examples each: all ten positive with Gini 0, seven positive and three negative with Gini 0.42, and five of each with Gini 0.5. The second plots Gini against the share of positives as an arch that is 0 at both ends and 0.5 in the middle.
diagram.caption: Gini impurity for nodes of ten examples. Use the buttons to compare three nodes and then see the whole curve.

lead.text: A node holds 10 examples, of which 9 are positive and 1 is negative. Work out its Gini impurity, 1 minus the sum of the squared class shares.

reveal.text: The node is nearly pure, so the value is close to 0.

lead.text: A question sends 5 examples to the left child, all positive, and 5 examples to the right child, of which 2 are positive and 3 are negative. The right child has a Gini of 0.48. Both children hold half the examples, and a pure child has a Gini of 0. Predict the weighted average Gini of the two children.

reveal.text: The weights are the shares of the examples, one half each, and one child contributes nothing.

steps.headline: A split is scored by how far it lowers the weighted impurity of the children below that of the parent.

lead.text: Each child is weighted by its share of the examples, so a large mixed child counts for more than a small one. The **weighted child impurity** is the sum of each child's share times its Gini, and the **gain**, the impurity decrease, is the parent's Gini minus that sum. For the split on income the left child has 5 of the 10 loans and G = 0, the right child has the other 5 and G = 0.48, so the weighted impurity is 0.5 × 0 + 0.5 × 0.48 = 0.24 and the gain is 0.42 − 0.24 = 0.18.

afterFigure.text: A split on age sends 6 loans left (4 positive, 2 negative, G = 0.444) and 4 right (3 positive, 1 negative, G = 0.375), which gives a weighted impurity of 0.417 and a gain of only about 0.003. The tree takes the question with the largest gain, here income, and then repeats the search inside each child, which is why trees are built greedily, one question at a time.

diagram.alt: A decision tree stump for a node of 10 loans, 7 positive and 3 negative, with Gini 0.42. Split A asks if income is at least 40 thousand and sends 5 positive and 0 negative left and 2 positive and 3 negative right, with weighted Gini 0.24. Split B asks if age is under 30 and sends 4 positive and 2 negative left and 3 positive and 1 negative right, with weighted Gini 0.417.

steps.headline: Score a third question for the same node: it sends 7 loans left (6 positive, 1 negative) and 3 right (1 positive, 2 negative).

workedSteps.text: The left child has Gini 1 − (6/7)² − (1/7)².
The right child has Gini 1 − (1/3)² − (2/3)².
Weight each child by its share of the 10 loans, 7 out of 10 and 3 out of 10, and add.
Subtract that from the parent's impurity.

steps.headline: Compute the gain of the split on age, which sends 6 loans left (4 positive, 2 negative) and 4 loans right (3 positive, 1 negative).

workedSteps.text: The left child has Gini 1 − (4/6)² − (2/6)², and the right has 1 − (3/4)² − (1/4)².
The weights are 6/10 and 4/10.
Subtract the weighted child impurity from the parent's 0.42, and give the gain to three decimal places.

steps.headline: A tree grown until every leaf is pure fits its training examples exactly, and it changes a great deal when the examples change.

lead.text: Nothing in the splitting rule stops a tree. Left to run, it keeps asking questions until every leaf holds examples of one class, so that its training accuracy is 1, the same condition that made the degree-9 polynomial score zero error and fail on new data. A deep tree has memorised its examples, including the noise in them, and a different sample of the same population would produce a quite different tree.

afterFigure.text: That sensitivity is the variance of the last module, and averaging is a way to reduce it. If many models were each fitted to a different sample and their answers were combined, the quirks of any one would be outvoted. The difficulty is that the data provide only one sample, which is where the bootstrap comes in.

steps.headline: Bagging fits many trees to resampled data and takes a vote, and the vote helps only because the trees differ.

lead.text: A **bootstrap sample** is made by drawing rows from the training set *with replacement* until it has as many rows as the original, so some rows appear twice and some not at all. **Bagging** fits one deep tree to each of many bootstrap samples and lets them vote, 1 or 0, with the majority deciding. In the figure five trees vote 1, 0, 1, 1 and 0, and the forest predicts 1. Leo Breiman's random forests paper of 2001 added a second source of difference: at every split a tree considers only a random subset of the features, which makes the trees less alike still.

afterFigure.text: The trees must differ, because a vote of identical copies is just one tree. If three models were each right 70% of the time and their errors were independent, the majority would be right 3 × 0.7² × 0.3 + 0.7³ = 0.784 of the time, better than any one. Real trees do not err independently, so the gain is smaller, but both resampling and feature subsets exist to push in that direction.

lead.text: A bootstrap sample of 5 rows is drawn with replacement from a training set of 5 rows. Each draw picks one of the 5 rows at random. What is the probability that one particular row is not picked in any of the 5 draws?

reveal.text: The chance of missing the row on one draw is 4 in 5, and the draws are independent.

steps.headline: The rows a bootstrap sample leaves out form a free validation set for that tree.

lead.text: The chance that a given row is missed by a bootstrap sample of n rows is (1 − 1/n)ⁿ, which for n = 20 is 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.36 and which settles at about 0.368 as n grows. Each tree therefore leaves out roughly a third of the rows, called its **out-of-bag** rows, and it never saw them.

afterFigure.text: Scoring each row only with the trees that did not see it gives an honest estimate of the forest's accuracy without setting a validation set aside. It is the same idea as cross-validation, obtained as a by-product of training. The forest is still tested once on the untouched test set at the end.

lead.text: A tree is grown with no limit on its depth, and it reaches a training accuracy of 1.0.

reveal.text: A training score of 1 is what memorisation also produces, so it settles nothing by itself.

lead.text: Three models each classify an example correctly with probability 0.7, and their errors are independent. A majority vote is correct when at least two of the three are correct. What is the probability that the vote is correct?

reveal.text: Add the probability of exactly two correct, 3 × 0.7² × 0.3, to that of all three correct, 0.7³.

lessons.orientation: Choose a split by Gini impurity and explain why a vote of many different trees beats one deep tree.
lessons.nextAction: Build a single artificial neuron, run a forward pass by hand, and count the parameters in a small network.

blocks.text: A node in a decision tree holds 10 loans, 7 of which were repaid and 3 were not, and a tree has to choose a question that separates them better. Asking whether income is at least 40 thousand sends five loans, all repaid, one way and five loans, two repaid and three not, the other. Asking whether the applicant is under 30 barely helps. A number computed from the counts alone, the Gini impurity, says by how much: 0.18 for the first question and 0.003 for the second.

That is all a tree needs to grow. What it gives, grown deep, is a model that has memorised its examples, and the second half of this lesson shows how a vote of many trees fitted to resampled data repairs the weakness.

The first shows three nodes of ten examples each: all ten positive with Gini 0, seven positive and three negative with Gini 0.42, and five of each with Gini 0.5. The second plots Gini against the share of positives as an arch that is 0 at both ends and 0.5 in the middle.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute Gini impurity and the gain of a split, and explain why a forest of different trees beats a single deep tree.
intro.whyItMatters: Forests of trees are among the strongest general-purpose models for tables of data.

recap.keyIdea: A tree picks the question that lowers the weighted Gini impurity the most, and a random forest averages many trees grown on resampled data so that their individual quirks are outvoted.

blocks.text: You computed the Gini impurity of a node, weighted the impurity of two children by their sizes, and found the gain, which a tree uses to choose each question. A deep tree memorises, and a vote of trees fitted to bootstrap samples, with features drawn at random at each split, reduces that variance because the trees differ.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to a different family of model, in which a single unit multiplies its inputs by weights, and units are stacked into networks.

lessons.title: Neural networks from one neuron up

steps.headline: A neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function.

lead.text: The straight-line model of the first lesson, ŷ = w·x + b, extends to several inputs by giving each input its own weight, so that **z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b**. A unit that computes this sum and then applies a function f to it, **a = f(z)**, is a **neuron**. Take the weights 1.5 and −1 and the bias −1. With the inputs 3 and 2 the weighted sum is 4.5 − 2 − 1 = 1.5, and with the inputs 2 and 3 it is 3 − 3 − 1 = −1.

afterFigure.text: The weights and the bias are the parameters, and they are learned in the same way as before, by reducing a loss. The new part is the function f, the **activation**. What a neuron outputs depends on which activation is used, and the figure shows the value after two common ones, which the next screens explain.

diagram.alt: A single neuron. Two inputs x1 and x2 are multiplied by the weights 1.5 and minus 1, added to the bias minus 1 to give z, and passed through an activation f. With inputs 3 and 2, z is 1.5, ReLU gives 1.5 and sigmoid gives 0.8176. With inputs 2 and 3, z is minus 1, ReLU gives 0 and sigmoid gives 0.2689.

lead.text: A neuron has weights 1.5 and −1 and a bias of −1. For the inputs x₁ = 1 and x₂ = 4, work out z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b.

reveal.text: Multiply each input by its own weight before adding the bias.

lead.text: The sigmoid activation computes 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z)), where e^0 = 1. A sigmoid neuron has z = 0. Predict its output.

reveal.text: The sigmoid is centred on 0, and it maps every z to a value between 0 and 1.

steps.headline: An activation bends the neuron's output, and ReLU and sigmoid are the two most common bends.

lead.text: The **ReLU**, short for rectified linear unit, is the simplest: **ReLU(z) = max(0, z)**, so a negative z gives 0 and a positive z passes through unchanged. For the two neurons on the earlier screen, z = 1.5 gives 1.5 and z = −1 gives 0. The **sigmoid**, **σ(z) = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z))**, squeezes every z into the range between 0 and 1, so that σ(0) = 0.5, σ(1.5) = 0.8176 and σ(−1) = 0.2689, and it is the natural choice for an output that is read as a probability.

afterFigure.text: The two curves are not straight lines, and that is their whole purpose. The sigmoid flattens out for large positive and large negative z, so a very confident neuron changes slowly, and ReLU is flat on one side and straight on the other, which makes it cheap and the usual choice inside a network. Both are applied one neuron at a time, to the z that neuron computed.

diagram.alt: Two plots of activation functions for z from minus 4 to 4. ReLU is 0 for negative z and equals z for positive z, with marked points at z minus 1 giving 0 and z 1.5 giving 1.5. Sigmoid is an S-shaped curve rising from near 0 to near 1, equal to 0.5 at z 0, with marked points at z minus 1 giving 0.2689 and z 1.5 giving 0.8176.
diagram.caption: ReLU and sigmoid, with the two values of z from the neuron on the last screen marked.

steps.headline: A layer is several neurons that all read the same inputs, and a network's parameters are its weights and biases.

lead.text: Putting several neurons side by side gives a **layer**, and feeding one layer's outputs into the next gives a network. In a **fully connected** layer every neuron reads every output of the layer before, so a layer from 3 values to 4 neurons has 3 × 4 = 12 weights, and each of the 4 neurons has one bias, which makes 16 parameters. A second layer from those 4 values to 1 neuron adds 4 × 1 + 1 = 5.

afterFigure.text: The rule is that a layer with n inputs and m neurons has **n × m + m** parameters, and a network's count is the sum over its layers. The 3-4-1 network has 21. The count matters because each parameter has to be learned from data, and a network with more parameters than examples can memorise them in the way of the degree-9 polynomial.

diagram.alt: A fully connected network with 3 inputs, a hidden layer of 4 neurons and 1 output neuron, with a line from every unit to every unit in the next layer. The second view colours the 12 first-layer connections and the 4 second-layer connections and counts the parameters: 3 times 4 plus 4 biases is 16, 4 times 1 plus 1 is 5, 21 in all.

lead.text: A fully connected network has layer sizes 5, 2 and 1, with a bias for every neuron: 5 inputs, a hidden layer of 2 neurons and 1 output neuron. How many parameters does it have?

reveal.text: Count each layer separately: its inputs times its neurons, plus one bias per neuron.

steps.headline: Without an activation between them, stacked layers collapse into a single linear map.

lead.text: Suppose the first layer computes h = 2x + 1 and the second computes y = 3h − 4, with no activation in between. Substituting gives y = 3(2x + 1) − 4 = 6x − 1, which is one straight line with one weight and one bias. However many layers are stacked, the result is a single line, so depth adds nothing at all.

afterFigure.text: Putting a ReLU between the layers changes that. The output becomes y = 3·ReLU(2x + 1) − 4, which is flat at −4 until 2x + 1 reaches 0 at x = −0.5, and then rises along the line. Each bend is built from a neuron, and many neurons together can approximate a curve of almost any shape, which is the source of a network's power.

diagram.alt: The output y of a two-layer network as a function of x. Without an activation between the layers it is the straight line y equals 6x minus 1. With a ReLU between the layers it is flat at minus 4 for x below minus 0.5 and then rises along the same slope.
diagram.caption: Two layers with and without an activation between them. Use the buttons to compare the shape of the output.

lead.text: The first layer computes h = 2x + 1 and the second computes y = 3h − 4, with no activation between them. Work out y when x = 5.

reveal.text: Compute h from x first, and then y from h.

steps.headline: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss for every weight, by applying the chain rule from the output backwards.

lead.text: Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, and for a network the loss depends on a weight only through a chain of layers. Take the chain x → h = w₁·x → ŷ = w₂·h → L = ½(ŷ − 4)², with x = 2, w₁ = 1 and w₂ = 3. The forward pass gives h = 2, ŷ = 6 and L = 2. Going backward, dL/dŷ = ŷ − 4 = 2, and then **dL/dw₂ = dL/dŷ × h = 2 × 2 = 4**.

afterFigure.text: Each earlier gradient reuses the one after it: dL/dh = dL/dŷ × w₂ = 2 × 3 = 6, and **dL/dw₁ = dL/dh × x = 6 × 2 = 12**. This reuse is **backpropagation**, a method for computing the gradients and not a separate way of learning, since the update is still w ← w − η · gradient. Rosenblatt's perceptron dates from 1958, and Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularised backpropagation for multi-layer networks in *Nature* in 1986.

diagram.alt: A small computation graph. The input x is 2 and w1 is 1, giving h equal to 2. Then w2 is 3, giving the prediction y-hat equal to 6, and the loss one half of y-hat minus 4 squared, equal to 2. The second view shows the gradients flowing backward: dL by d y-hat is 2, dL by dw2 is 4, dL by dh is 6 and dL by dw1 is 12.
diagram.caption: The forward pass computes the loss. The backward pass works out how the loss changes with each weight.

steps.headline: Take one gradient step on the chain above, with learning rate η = 0.01 and the gradients dL/dw₂ = 4 and dL/dw₁ = 12.

workedSteps.text: The update for each weight is the weight minus η times its gradient. Start with w₂.
The first weight has a much larger gradient, so it moves further.
With the new weights the forward pass gives h = 0.88 × 2 = 1.76 and ŷ = 2.96 × 1.76 = 5.2096.
The loss has fallen from 2 to ½ × (5.2096 − 4)² ≈ 0.73.

steps.headline: Update w₂ for the same chain after a different forward pass: now dL/dw₂ = 8, w₂ = 2 and η = 0.05.

workedSteps.text: The update rule is the same as for any weight, w ← w − η · gradient.
Multiply the learning rate by the gradient.
Subtract that from the weight w₂ = 2 to get the new value.

reveal.text: Ask what each one produces: a gradient or an update.

lessons.nextAction: Chain the steps of a training run into a pipeline, and record enough about each run to reproduce it.

blocks.text: Two layers that each compute a straight line, h = 2x + 1 and then y = 3h − 4, produce y = 6x − 1, which is one straight line again. Adding a third layer, or a hundredth, gives the same result, so stacking them achieves nothing. Put a ReLU between the layers and the output bends at x = −0.5, flat to the left of it and rising to the right, and each such bend is something a network can build from.

This lesson builds the network from its smallest part, one neuron with weights, a bias and an activation, counts the parameters of a larger one, and then shows how the gradient of the loss reaches each weight.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to run a forward pass through a neuron, count the parameters of a small network, and say what backpropagation computes.
intro.whyItMatters: Neural networks sit behind most of the models you will meet in the next courses.

recap.keyIdea: A neuron applies an activation to a weighted sum, layers of them need that activation to be more than one linear map, and backpropagation delivers the gradients that gradient descent uses.

blocks.text: You computed z = w·x + b for a neuron, applied ReLU and sigmoid to it, counted n × m + m parameters per layer, and saw that layers without an activation collapse to one line. Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards to give each weight its gradient, and the update afterwards is the same gradient descent as before.

lessons.title: Pipelines and experiment tracking

steps.headline: A result that cannot be traced to its code, data and settings cannot be trusted or repeated.

lead.text: A notebook run on Monday scores 0.81. On Thursday the same notebook, run again after some edits, scores 0.84, and nobody can say whether the rise is real, because the data may have been refreshed, a parameter changed, or a random split fallen differently. The model file from Thursday exists, but nothing says what it was trained on.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is to turn the notebook's steps into a **pipeline**: a script that runs the data, validation, split, features, training and evaluation steps in a fixed order, so that every run follows the same path and each step can write down what it used. Sculley and colleagues observed in 2015 that the model code is only a small part of a real machine-learning system, and that most of the effort, and the debt, lies in the pipeline and infrastructure around it.

diagram.alt: A row of seven boxes joined by arrows: data, validate, split, features, train, evaluate and register. The first view says one script runs every step in order. The second view lists what each step records: the data hash, a check report, row ids per split, the feature code version, parameters and seed, metrics, and the model with its run id.

steps.headline: A run record names everything that could have changed the result.

lead.text: For each run the pipeline writes a **run record**, which has to name the code (the commit identifier), the data (an identifier that changes when the data changes), the parameters, the random seed, the software environment and the resulting metrics. A record such as *commit abc123, data hash 9f2c, learning rate 0.1, depth 4, seed 42, F1 0.81* lets a colleague, or you in six months, run the same thing again and expect the same number.

afterFigure.text: Storing runs in a shared **experiment tracker** makes them comparable: two runs can be set side by side, and the fields that differ are the candidates for any difference in score. The model that comes out of the best run goes into a **model registry** with the identifier of that run attached, so that every model in use can be traced back to how it was made.

lead.text: Run A has commit abc123, data hash 9f2c, seed 42, learning rate 0.1 and score 0.81. Run B has commit abc123, data hash 51d7, seed 42, learning rate 0.1 and score 0.84. Type the name of the field that differs, from commit, data hash, seed and learning rate.

reveal.text: Compare the two records field by field and look for the one that changed.

steps.headline: A content hash identifies a dataset by its bytes, and a seed fixes randomness only as far as the software behaves the same way.

lead.text: Data changes quietly, so naming a file `train.csv` identifies nothing. A **hash** function reads the bytes of the data and produces a short fingerprint: SHA-256 gives 64 hexadecimal characters, the same bytes always give the same fingerprint, and changing a single byte gives a completely different one. Storing the fingerprint in the run record says exactly which data a result came from, and it shows at once when the data has changed.

afterFigure.text: The **random seed** fixes the sequence of random numbers, so that splits and initial weights repeat. It is necessary, and it is not enough: a different version of a library may draw numbers in a different order, and some operations on a graphics card run in an order that varies between runs. That is why the environment, with library versions, belongs in the record, and why reproducing a number may mean matching the machine type as well.

lead.text: A search will try 3 learning rates and 4 tree depths, every combination of the two. Predict how many different configurations that is.

reveal.text: Every learning rate is paired with every depth.

steps.headline: A grid search fits one model for every configuration and every fold, so the work multiplies.

lead.text: Tuning settings with cross-validation fits a model for each configuration on each fold, so the number of fits is **configurations × folds**. With 3 learning rates, 4 depths and 5 folds that is 3 × 4 × 5 = 60 fits, and adding a fourth setting with 3 values would multiply it by 3, to 180. A grid grows quickly, which is why the choice of what to tune matters.

afterFigure.text: Once the best configuration is chosen, one further fit on all the training data gives the final model, so the total is 61. The cost is mostly time, and the fits are independent of one another, so they can be run in parallel: 60 fits that take 2 minutes each need 120 minutes one after another, and 30 minutes on 4 machines at once. A pipeline that records every fit makes the search repeatable and spares you from repeating the work.

lead.text: A search tries 5 learning rates and 2 depths, each combination scored with 3-fold cross-validation. How many model fits does that need, not counting a final refit?

reveal.text: Multiply the number of configurations by the number of folds.

steps.headline: Count the fits for 2 learning rates and 3 depths with 4-fold cross-validation, including the final refit.

workedSteps.text: The configurations are every learning rate with every depth.
Each configuration is fitted once for each fold.
The winning configuration is then fitted once more on all the training data.
If each fit takes 3 minutes, the search is 72 minutes before the refit, and the refit adds 3.

steps.headline: Count the fits for 2 optimisers, 3 learning rates and 2 depths with 3-fold cross-validation.

workedSteps.text: The configurations are every combination of the three settings.
Each is fitted on each of the 3 folds.
Work out the number of fits, not counting a final refit.

steps.headline: Automation is the point of a pipeline, and Google's MLOps guide describes it in levels.

lead.text: The Google Cloud guide on continuous delivery and automation of machine learning describes three levels. At level 0 every step is manual: the data scientist runs a notebook, hands over a model file, and an engineer deploys it. At level 1 the training pipeline is automated, so that the model can be retrained on new data by running the pipeline again. At level 2 the pipeline's own code is tested and deployed automatically, which makes changes to it as routine as changes to any other software.

afterFigure.text: Each level removes a kind of manual work, and with it a kind of mistake. A pipeline that retrains on fresh data without a person depends entirely on the checks inside it, the validation of the data and the comparison with the current model, so those checks are where a team builds its confidence.

lead.text: A team sets the random seed to 42 on two machines, and the scores of the two runs still differ in the second decimal place.

reveal.text: The seed controls only the random numbers, and other things could differ.

lead.text: A search needs 48 model fits, and each fit takes 5 minutes. The fits run 4 at a time on 4 workers. How many minutes does the whole search take?

reveal.text: Divide the fits among the workers first, then multiply by the time one fit takes.

lessons.orientation: Say what must be recorded to reproduce a training run and count the fits in a hyperparameter search.
lessons.nextAction: Put a model behind a service, split a latency budget, and size the number of copies the load requires.

blocks.text: On Monday a notebook scores 0.81. On Thursday, after some edits, it scores 0.84, and the Thursday model file is saved in a folder. Whether the extra three points are real depends on whether the code, the data, the settings, the random split or the software changed, and none of that was written down. A score on its own is a claim that nobody can check.

A pipeline repeats the same steps in the same order each time, and a run record writes down what each step used. This lesson sets out what the record has to hold and counts the cost of the searches that fill a tracker with runs.

recap.keyIdea: A pipeline runs the same steps each time, and a run record naming the code, data hash, parameters, seed, environment and metrics makes a result repeatable.

blocks.text: You turned a notebook into pipeline steps, listed the fields a run record needs, and used a hash to identify data by its bytes. A seed helps but does not make a run repeatable on its own, and a grid search costs configurations times folds in fits, with one more for the final model.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the finished model out of the tracker and puts it behind a service, where latency and load decide how it has to be run.

lessons.title: Serving a model and releasing it safely

steps.headline: Predictions can be computed ahead of time in a batch or on demand for each request, and the choice follows from when the answer is needed.

lead.text: In **batch** serving a job scores every row on a schedule, say every night, and stores the results in a table that other systems read. It suits any case in which the prediction is needed in advance and the inputs are known beforehand, such as a recommendation list for each customer, and it needs no fast service: a job that scores 1.2 million rows at 400 rows per second takes 3,000 seconds, which is 50 minutes.

afterFigure.text: **Online** serving scores each request when it arrives, and it is needed when the input exists only at that moment, such as a card payment to be approved or declined. The model then sits behind a service with a response-time requirement, and everything the model needs has to be fetched within it. The trade is between the staleness of batch scores, which can be a day old, and the cost and difficulty of keeping a service fast and available.

diagram.alt: Two ways of serving. In the batch view a nightly job scores every customer ahead of time and stores a table of scores that an application reads later. In the online view a request arrives, a model service scores it immediately, and the score returns within a fraction of a second.

lead.text: A nightly batch job scores 1.2 million rows at 400 rows per second. How many minutes does the job take?

reveal.text: First work out the time in seconds, and then convert it.

steps.headline: An online request has a fixed time budget, and every step on its path draws from it.

lead.text: A payment check that must answer within 150 milliseconds has to fit the whole request path into that time: the network journey in and out, the lookup of the features the model needs, and the model's own computation. If the network takes 30 ms and the feature lookup takes 45 ms, the model has 150 − 30 − 45 = 75 ms, and a model that needs 100 ms makes every request late.

afterFigure.text: Budgets are usually set on a high **percentile** of latency, such as the 99th, and not on the average, because the slow requests are the ones that users notice and that time out. This makes the model's size a design decision: a larger model may be more accurate offline and still not fit in the time its steps leave.

lead.text: A request has a budget of 120 ms. The network takes 25 ms and the feature lookup takes 40 ms. How many milliseconds are left for the model?

reveal.text: Subtract both of the other steps from the budget.

lead.text: A service must handle 300 requests per second at its peak, and each replica of the model can handle 100 requests per second. Predict how many replicas are needed if each one is to run at full capacity.

reveal.text: Full capacity leaves nothing spare for a burst or for a replica that fails, which the next screen takes up.

steps.headline: Replicas are sized from the peak load, the capacity of one replica and a target utilisation below 100%.

lead.text: A **replica** is one running copy of the service, and capacity is added by running more of them. The number needed is **peak load ÷ (capacity per replica × target utilisation)**, rounded up. For a peak of 900 requests per second and replicas that each handle 60, running at full capacity needs 900 ÷ 60 = 15, while a target of 75% needs 900 ÷ (60 × 0.75) = 20.

afterFigure.text: The extra replicas buy headroom. Waiting time rises sharply as a server nears full utilisation, so a replica run at 100% answers slowly even when it is coping, and a burst of traffic or the loss of a replica pushes the others over. The result is rounded *up*, since a fraction of a replica cannot be run and rounding down would exceed the target.

diagram.alt: Two rows of replica bars. The first view shows 15 replicas each filled to the top, which carries the peak load of 900 requests per second with no spare room. The second view shows 20 replicas each filled to three quarters, carrying the same load with a quarter of each replica spare.

steps.headline: Size a service for a peak of 500 requests per second, replicas that each handle 40, and a target utilisation of 70%.

workedSteps.text: Each replica should carry 70% of its capacity at the peak.
Divide the peak load by that usable capacity.
Round up, since 17 replicas would carry more than 70% of capacity each.
At 18 replicas the utilisation at peak is 500 ÷ (18 × 40) ≈ 69%, just under the target.

steps.headline: Size a service for a peak of 1,000 requests per second, replicas that each handle 80, and a target utilisation of 80%.

workedSteps.text: The usable capacity of one replica is 80 × 0.8.
Divide the peak by it.
Round up to a whole number of replicas.

steps.headline: A model that passes offline evaluation can still fail in production when the features it sees differ from those it learned on.

lead.text: The scores from the test set describe the model on the features as the *training* pipeline computed them. If the serving code computes a feature differently, the model sees values it was not trained on, and the offline score no longer applies. This is **train-serve skew**. A typical cause is two definitions of one feature, for instance an average over 30 days in a SQL query for training and over 7 days in application code for serving, and another is a unit change, such as days in training and hours in serving.

afterFigure.text: The defences are to use one feature definition in both places, as in the second view, and to log the features that serving actually uses so that their distributions can be compared with the training data. A model that was checked offline has not yet been checked in production, and that is what the release steps in the next section are for.

diagram.alt: Two ways of building one feature. In the first view the training pipeline computes the average basket over 30 days in SQL while the serving code computes it over 7 days in Python, so the model sees shifted values. In the second view a single shared feature definition feeds both training and serving.
diagram.caption: Two feature definitions and one shared definition. Use the buttons to compare them.

steps.headline: A new model is released in stages, each of which limits how many users a fault can reach.

lead.text: In a **shadow** deployment the candidate receives a copy of live traffic and its answers are logged but never returned, so it can be compared with the current model on real requests without affecting any user. In a **canary** release a small share of requests, such as 5%, is answered by the candidate, while the rest stay on the current model. If the error rate, the latency and the business measure stay within limits, the share is raised in steps up to 100%.

afterFigure.text: The stages are only useful if there is a way back. A **rollback** sends traffic to the previous model again, and it works only if the previous model is still deployed and still compatible with the features and schemas now in place, which is not guaranteed when the new release also changed the features. Keeping the old model and its feature code ready is part of the release plan.

diagram.alt: A router splits requests between the current model and a candidate. In shadow mode every request is served by the current model and a copy goes to the candidate, whose answers are only logged. In a canary release 5 percent of requests are served by the candidate. In the full rollout all requests go to the candidate and the current model is kept ready for rollback.
diagram.caption: Three stages of a release. Use the buttons to follow a new model from shadow to full traffic.

reveal.text: Two per cent is 0.02 of the traffic.

lead.text: A service peaks at 400 requests per second, with replicas that each handle 50 requests per second and a target utilisation of 80%. A 5% canary candidate takes 5% of the peak. How many replicas does the candidate need?

reveal.text: The candidate's share is 5% of 400, and the same sizing formula applies to it, rounded up.

lessons.orientation: Choose batch or online serving, size replicas for a latency target and describe a canary release.
lessons.reviewLabel: Serving a model and releasing it safely
lessons.nextAction: Watch a model after release: compare live feature distributions with training and decide what to monitor when labels arrive late.

blocks.text: A payment check has 150 milliseconds in which to answer, and its path has three steps: the network takes 30, the feature lookup takes 45, and the model has 75. A model that needs 100 makes every request late, however accurate it was on the test set, and that accuracy was in any case measured on features that the serving code may compute differently.

Serving a model is a set of arithmetic and design decisions that sit outside the model, about latency, about how many copies to run at peak, and about how to let a new version meet real traffic without exposing everyone to its faults. This lesson works through them.

intro.whyItMatters: These decisions decide whether a good model can be used at all.

recap.keyIdea: Serving is chosen by when the answer is needed, latency and replicas follow from the budget and the peak load, and a staged release limits how far a fault can spread.

blocks.text: You chose between scoring ahead of time and scoring on request, split a latency budget across a request path, and sized replicas as peak load ÷ (capacity × target utilisation), rounded up. A model is released through shadow and canary stages, with a rollback that is only as good as the compatibility of the old model with the current features.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what happens after release, when live data slowly stops resembling the data the model was trained on.

lessons.title: Monitoring and drift

steps.headline: A model's inputs can shift without any error being raised, and the model keeps answering as if nothing had happened.

lead.text: Once a model is in production the world keeps moving. Suppose the order value of customers was cut at its quartiles when the model was trained, so that each of four bins held 25% of the orders. A week later the bins hold 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%, because orders have become smaller, and the model, which has never seen so many small orders, goes on answering without any sign of strain. A change in the distribution of the inputs is called **data drift**.

afterFigure.text: Drift does not raise an error. The service stays up, latency stays flat and predictions keep coming out, so it has to be looked for with a measure. A second kind of change is different in cause, and it is taken up later in the lesson: the *relationship* between the inputs and the label can change while the inputs themselves look the same.

lead.text: The population stability index compares the share of live rows in each bin with the share seen in training. Predict its value when the live shares equal the training shares in every bin.

reveal.text: A measure of change should say that nothing has changed when the two distributions agree.

steps.headline: The population stability index adds up, bin by bin, how far the live shares have moved from the training shares.

lead.text: For each bin let e be the expected share, from training, and a the actual share, from live data. The **population stability index** is **PSI = Σ (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e)**, summed over the bins. Each term is zero when a = e, and positive when a differs from e in either direction, because (a − e) and ln(a ÷ e) always have the same sign. The index is therefore never negative, and a larger value means a larger shift.

afterFigure.text: For the four bins above the terms are 0.0705, 0.0091, 0.0112 and 0.1374, which add up to a PSI of 0.228. The last term dominates, since the highest bin has lost more than half of its share, from 25% to 10%. Looking at the terms says *where* the shift is, and not only how large it is, which is the useful part for finding the cause.

The second view adds each bin's contribution to the population stability index, 0.0705, 0.0091, 0.0112 and 0.1374, which sum to 0.228.

lead.text: A feature has two bins. In training they hold 70% and 30% of the rows, and in the live week 60% and 40%. Work out the PSI, to three decimal places, using PSI = Σ (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e).

reveal.text: Work out the term for each bin separately, then add them.

steps.headline: The usual PSI thresholds of 0.1 and 0.25 are conventions, and they say nothing about whether the model is hurt.

lead.text: The values that are quoted are that a PSI below 0.1 means little change, from 0.1 to 0.25 a moderate change worth a look, and above 0.25 a large one. These are conventions from credit-risk practice and not laws: no theorem puts the boundary at 0.25, and a feature can have a large PSI and little effect on the model, or a small PSI and a large one. They serve as a starting alarm, to be tuned against what you observe.

afterFigure.text: The number of bins and their width also matter, since the same data gives different PSI values under different binning, which is why the bins are fixed once from the training data and reused. A shift in one feature that the model barely uses is less urgent than a shift in the feature it depends on most. The PSI says that a distribution has moved. It does not say that predictions have worsened, which only labels can show.

steps.headline: Work out the PSI for three bins with expected shares 0.4, 0.4 and 0.2 and actual shares 0.3, 0.4 and 0.3.

workedSteps.text: The first bin has moved down by 0.1, from 0.4 to 0.3.
The second bin has not moved, so its term is zero.
The third bin has moved up by 0.1, from 0.2 to 0.3.
Add the three terms.

steps.headline: Work out the PSI for two bins with expected shares 0.5 and 0.5 and actual shares 0.3 and 0.7.

workedSteps.text: The first bin has fallen from 0.5 to 0.3.
The second bin has risen from 0.5 to 0.7, and its term is (0.7 − 0.5) × ln(0.7 ÷ 0.5).
Add the two terms, and give the PSI to three decimal places.

steps.headline: Data drift, concept drift and label delay are different problems, and each needs a different watch.

lead.text: **Data drift** is a change in the inputs, and the PSI measures it. **Concept drift** is a change in what the inputs mean for the label: customers change what they buy, so the same features now imply a different outcome, and the model's rule is out of date while the inputs look exactly as before. A PSI on the inputs cannot see it, and only the labels can, by showing the accuracy fall.

afterFigure.text: The labels may be slow to arrive. A fraud label arrives when a chargeback does, a default label arrives months after a loan, and with a **label delay** of 30 days the accuracy of today's predictions cannot be computed until next month. Input drift tends to appear first for that reason, and 'accuracy is stable' may only mean that the accuracy of old predictions is stable.

diagram.alt: Three kinds of change after release. In data drift the distribution of an input shifts while its relationship to the label holds. In concept drift the inputs look the same while the relationship to the label changes, shown by a flatter line against the original dashed one. In label delay a prediction on day 0 is scored only when its label arrives on day 30.
diagram.caption: Data drift, concept drift and label delay compared. Use the buttons to see each.

lead.text: A new camera makes every product photo brighter. A bright photo of a shoe is still a shoe, so what the photo means has not changed, only how the photos are distributed. Is this data drift or concept drift? Type the name.

reveal.text: Ask whether the input distribution changed, the relationship to the label changed, or both.

steps.headline: While labels are late, monitor what is available now: inputs, predictions and business outcomes.

lead.text: Three kinds of signal are available straight away. The **input distributions** of each feature, tracked with a measure such as the PSI each day, show data drift. The **prediction distribution**, such as the share of rows flagged positive, shows how the model's behaviour has changed. **Data quality** checks, such as the share of missing values and the range of each feature, catch a broken upstream feed, which is the commonest cause of a sudden shift.

afterFigure.text: Business outcomes that arrive faster than the label, such as the rate of customer complaints or manual review overturns, act as proxies. When the labels do arrive they are matched back to the predictions, and the accuracy is computed for the period they cover. In the figure, which is illustrative, the PSI crosses 0.1 about a week before it crosses 0.25, and the prediction rate has been rising since the same time, and both give weeks of warning before any label could.

diagram.alt: Two line charts of illustrative data over 30 days. The daily population stability index of one feature stays below 0.1 until about day 18, passes 0.1, and passes 0.25 by about day 26. The share of predictions that are positive rises from about 5 percent to about 8 percent over the last 15 days.
diagram.caption: What can be watched while labels are late. The data are illustrative, and the lines mark the conventional PSI levels 0.1 and 0.25.

lead.text: Predictions are made every day, and each label arrives exactly 30 days after its prediction. On day 45, accuracy is computed over every prediction whose label has arrived. Up to which day were those predictions made?

reveal.text: A prediction made on day d has its label on day d + 30.

lead.text: A feature is binned into three bins. In training they hold 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 of the rows, and in the live week 0.35, 0.45 and 0.2. Work out the PSI to three decimal places.

reveal.text: Work out one term per bin, (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e), and add them.

lessons.orientation: Compute a population stability index and decide what to monitor when labels arrive late.
lessons.nextAction: Compare a model's results across groups, write a model card, and place the work under the four NIST AI RMF functions.

blocks.text: The order value of customers was cut into four bins at training time, each holding 25% of the orders. One week after release the same bins hold 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%. The service is up, latency is flat, and every request returns an answer, and yet the model is being asked about a population that has shifted towards small orders, which it saw less often than it now sees them.

Nothing in the usual health checks reports this. It has to be measured against the distribution the model learned from, and when the labels that would show a fall in accuracy arrive a month late, the measures that work today are the ones on inputs and predictions.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a population stability index and decide what to monitor while labels are late.
intro.whyItMatters: Models degrade quietly, and the only defence is a measure you chose in advance.

recap.keyIdea: The PSI sums how far each bin's live share has moved from its training share, and while labels are late the inputs, the predictions and data quality are what can be watched.

blocks.text: You computed the PSI as the sum of (a − e) × ln(a ÷ e) over the bins, found that it is zero when nothing has shifted, and that the usual 0.1 and 0.25 levels are conventions. Data drift moves the inputs, concept drift moves their meaning, and label delay means accuracy lags both.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson asks a different kind of question about a model in use: whether it works as well for every group of people it affects, and how that is recorded.

lessons.title: Fairness, documentation and risk

steps.headline: A model can look fine on average and still treat groups of people differently, so its metrics have to be computed for each group.

lead.text: A lender's model approves 60 of 120 applicants in group X and 30 of 100 in group Y. The share of a group that receives the positive decision is its **selection rate**, which is 0.50 for X and 0.30 for Y. Asking for the same selection rate in every group is called **demographic parity**, and here the groups are 0.20 apart. Whether that gap is a fault depends on the situation, and the first step is to measure it, which an overall accuracy never does.

afterFigure.text: Selection rate ignores who actually deserved the decision. Of the 80 creditworthy applicants in group X, the model approved 52, and of the 50 in group Y it approved 25, so the share of qualified people who are found is 52 ÷ 80 = 0.65 for X and 25 ÷ 50 = 0.50 for Y. This is the **true positive rate**, the recall of the earlier lessons, and comparing it between groups is called **equal opportunity**. The gap is 0.15, a different gap from the 0.20 above.

Group Y has 100 applicants, 50 creditworthy, 30 selected and 25 of those creditworthy. The second view adds the selection rates, 0.50 and 0.30, and the true positive rates, 0.65 and 0.50.

lead.text: A model selects 40% of group A and 40% of group B, so demographic parity holds exactly. Among the people who deserved a positive decision, it finds 90% in group A and 60% in group B. Predict the gap in true positive rate.

reveal.text: Parity in one measure says nothing about the other, since the two measures divide by different counts.

steps.headline: Removing a protected attribute does not remove the bias, and the fairness measures cannot all be satisfied together.

lead.text: The attribute can be left out of the features, and its effect usually remains. A postcode, a first name or a pattern of purchases can be correlated with the attribute, so the model recovers it from them, and the bias in the labels it learned from comes through. The remedy is to keep the attribute available for *auditing*, so that the metrics can still be computed per group, even if the model is not given it.

afterFigure.text: The measures also conflict. When the groups have different base rates, a classifier can in general not equalise selection rates, true positive rates and precision at the same time, apart from special cases such as a perfect classifier, so a choice has to be made. The choice depends on what each kind of error costs the people affected, and it is a decision for the owners of the system and not a quantity that the data settles.

lead.text: A team removes the gender column from a hiring model's features and says the model can no longer be biased by gender.

reveal.text: Think about what other columns might carry information about the removed one.

steps.headline: A model card records what a model is for, what it was built from, and how it performs for each group.

lead.text: Measurements that stay in a notebook are lost when the model changes hands. Margaret Mitchell and colleagues proposed in 2019 that every released model should come with a short document, a **model card**, with nine sections: the model's details, its intended use, the factors it was evaluated on (such as groups), its metrics, its evaluation data, its training data, its quantitative analyses, ethical considerations, and caveats and recommendations.

afterFigure.text: The most useful entries are the plain limits. A card for a loan-ranking model says that it is meant to order applications for an officer to review and that automatic rejection is out of scope, it names the data it was evaluated on, and it reports the selection rate and true positive rate per group. A reader can then tell at once whether their use of the model is one it was built for.

lead.text: Type the name of the document that records a model's intended use, its data and its per-group metrics.

reveal.text: It was proposed by Mitchell and colleagues in 2019, and it works like a data sheet for a model.

steps.headline: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework divides risk work into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.

lead.text: NIST published version 1.0 of its Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework in January 2023, as a voluntary framework. Its core has four functions. **Govern** sets the policies, roles and culture that make risk work happen, and it runs across the other three. **Map** establishes the context and identifies the risks, **Measure** analyses and tracks them with metrics, and **Manage** prioritises the risks and acts on them.

afterFigure.text: The functions work as a way to sort the tasks of a project and to see what is missing. Writing a model's intended use belongs to Map, computing the per-group rates belongs to Measure, rolling back a failing release belongs to Manage, and naming an owner for each release belongs to Govern. A project that has plenty of Measure work and no Govern work has metrics and nobody responsible for acting on them.

diagram.alt: The four functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Govern is a bar across the top, covering the rest. Below it, Map, Measure and Manage follow one another. The second view maps four tasks to functions: writing intended use to Map, computing per-group true positive rate to Measure, rolling back a failing model to Manage, and assigning an owner to Govern.

steps.headline: Place four tasks under the AI RMF functions: write the intended use, compute per-group rates, roll back a failing release, name an owner.

workedSteps.text: The intended use and its limits describe the context in which the system will operate, and the risks that follow from it.
Computing a rate for each group is a measurement of a risk that has already been identified.
workedSteps.math: true positive rate per group: Measure

workedSteps.text: A rollback is an action taken once a risk has been prioritised and has come true.
workedSteps.math: roll back a failing release: Manage

workedSteps.text: Naming an owner is a matter of roles and accountability, which cuts across the other three.

steps.headline: Place the task 'record the model's training data and its known limits in a model card' under one of the four functions.

workedSteps.text: The task describes the system and the context it will be used in, so that its risks can be understood.
It does not analyse a risk with a metric, take action on a risk, or set policy.
Type the function, one of Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, to which the task belongs.

lessons.orientation: Compare a metric across groups, write what a model card must say, and place work under the four NIST AI RMF functions.
lessons.nextAction: You can now fit and evaluate a model honestly, ship it, watch it, and say who it serves and how well.

blocks.text: A lender's model approves 60 of the 120 applicants in group X and 30 of the 100 in group Y, which is a selection rate of 0.50 against 0.30. Of the people who deserved a loan, it finds 52 of 80 in group X and 25 of 50 in group Y, a rate of 0.65 against 0.50. An accuracy figure for the two groups together contains neither gap.

Metrics that are computed per group, a document that records what a model is for, and a framework for organising the work of managing its risk are the three tools of this lesson. They do not decide what is fair, which is a question for the people who own the system, and they make it possible to see the facts that decision has to rest on.
